key_rules: Never apply vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid) and retinoid in the same PM session
Avoid AHAs/BHAs on nights retinoid is applied
SPF is non-negotiable daily — UV causes 80% of facial aging
Increase retinoid frequency only after 4 weeks of tolerance at current schedule
Expect redness and peeling in weeks 1-4; this is expected, not a reason to stop
red_flags: Severe burning or blistering — discontinue retinoid and consult dermatologist
Persistent irritation beyond 8 weeks — reduce retinoid frequency
New hyperpigmentation — may indicate post-inflammatory response; review routine

weeks_1_2.label: Foundation phase
weeks_1_2.focus: Establish barrier tolerance before introducing actives
weeks_1_2.notes: No actives yet. Skin must be stable before retinoid introduction.
weeks_1_2.expect: Skin adjusting to new routine. No dramatic changes expected.

weeks_3_4.label: Retinoid introduction
weeks_3_4.focus: Begin retinoid 2x per week using sandwich method
weeks_3_4.notes: Sandwich method: moisturiser → retinoid → moisturiser. 2x per week only.
weeks_3_4.expect: Mild dryness or flaking normal. Purging possible weeks 3-6.

weeks_5_8.label: Retinoid escalation
weeks_5_8.focus: Increase to every other night. Alternate with recovery nights.
weeks_5_8.notes: Drop back to 2x/week if significant irritation persists.
weeks_5_8.expect: Purging resolves. Texture improvement begins. Some dryness still normal.

weeks_9_12.label: Active maintenance
weeks_9_12.focus: Retinoid nightly if tolerated. Add AHA 1-2x per week.
pm_steps: AHA 1-2x per week (not on retinoid nights)
weeks_9_12.notes: Never AHA and retinoid same night. SPF non-negotiable — retinoids cause photosensitivity.
weeks_9_12.expect: Visible improvement in fine lines and texture by week 10-12.

key_rules: Introduce tretinoin gradually (every 2–3 nights) to minimize purging and irritation
Never combine tretinoin and AHAs/BHAs in the same application
Apply SPF every morning without exception when using tretinoin
Isotretinoin is reserved for severe/nodulo-cystic or antibiotic-resistant acne — requires prescription

red_flags: Nodulo-cystic or scarring acne: refer for prescription evaluation including oral isotretinoin
Severe peeling, blistering, or chemical burn appearance: discontinue tretinoin immediately
No improvement after 12 weeks of consistent use: seek dermatology review
Hormonal flare pattern (perimenstrual): may require hormonal therapy assessment

weeks_1_2.label: Baseline phase
weeks_1_2.notes: Strip back everything first. Establish baseline tolerance.

weeks_3_4.label: BHA introduction
weeks_3_4.focus: Salicylic acid 2% on 2-3 nights per week
weeks_3_4.notes: Alternating nights. Not every night initially.
weeks_3_4.expect: Mild purging weeks 3-5 possible. Some initial dryness.

weeks_5_8.label: Retinoid introduction
weeks_5_8.notes: Never BHA and retinoid same night.
weeks_5_8.expect: Improvement in comedones and texture. Some purging still possible.

weeks_9_12.label: Optimisation
weeks_9_12.focus: Increase retinoid frequency. Add azelaic acid if PIH present.
weeks_9_12.notes: Azelaic acid safe AM and PM. Anti-inflammatory and reduces PIH.
weeks_9_12.expect: Significant reduction in active acne. PIH fading. Texture improving.

am_routine.reason: Avoid skin irritation which worsens hyperpigmentation
Antioxidant neutralizes ROS; complements UV protection
Solar protection is most important in hyperpigmentation management

pm_routine.reason: Avoid irritation to prevent post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
pm_routine.notes: Lukewarm water; avoid scrubbing or harsh physical exfoliation

pm_routine.reason: Inhibits tyrosinase; anti-inflammatory; effective for PIH

key_rules: Sunscreen daily is non-negotiable; UV exposure drives melanogenesis and reverses treatment gains
Do not combine azelaic acid and tretinoin on the same night initially; alternate to reduce irritation
Introduce tretinoin slowly (2-3 nights/week) and increase frequency only if well tolerated
Avoid any physical trauma or picking; PIH worsens with inflammation
Reassess at 6-12 weeks; melasma requires 6-12 months of consistent treatment
red_flags: Increasing redness, burning, or peeling — reduce tretinoin frequency immediately
New darker patches after starting treatment may indicate irritant PIH; stop aggravating agent
No improvement after 12 weeks warrants dermatologist review for prescription hydroquinone 2-4%
Avoid hydroquinone monobenzyl ether — can cause irreversible mottled depigmentation

weeks_1_2.label: Protection first
weeks_1_2.focus: SPF only — without it nothing else works
weeks_1_2.notes: UV exposure is the primary driver of hyperpigmentation. Every brightening active fails without SPF.

weeks_3_6.label: Brightening actives
weeks_3_6.notes: Vitamin C and niacinamide can be used together — niacin flushing reaction is a myth at standard concentrations.
weeks_3_6.expect: Gradual brightening. 8-12 weeks for visible change in dark spots.

weeks_7_10.label: Second brightening pathway
weeks_7_10.focus: Add tranexamic acid or azelaic acid
weeks_7_10.notes: Tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen-melanocyte interaction. Azelaic acid inhibits tyrosinase. Both safe long-term.
weeks_7_10.expect: Visible fading of PIH and melasma. 3 months minimum for deep pigmentation.

weeks_11_12.label: Retinoid addition
weeks_11_12.focus: Add retinoid 2x per week to accelerate cell turnover
weeks_11_12.notes: Retinoids accelerate pigment clearance via increased cell turnover. Not on AHA nights.
weeks_11_12.expect: Combination approach delivering meaningful results by week 12.

key_rules: Avoid all fragrance including essential oils — primary sensitizer for compromised barriers
Introduce one new product at a time, patch-test 48h on inner arm before full use
No AHAs, BHAs, or retinoids until barrier is fully restored (minimum 4 weeks)
Ceramide moisturizer must contain all three lipids: ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids
Reapply moisturizer after water exposure; do not allow skin to air-dry after washing
red_flags: Burning or stinging beyond 10 min after product application — discontinue immediately
Spreading redness or swelling — may indicate contact dermatitis, seek evaluation
Weeping, crusting, or oozing skin — potential infection, requires clinical assessment
No improvement in TEWL or hydration after 6 weeks — re-evaluate diagnosis

weeks_1_4.label: Full reset
weeks_1_4.focus: Stop ALL actives. Three products only.
weeks_1_4.notes: No actives for 4 weeks minimum. Slugging at night accelerates barrier recovery.
weeks_1_4.expect: Stinging and tightness reduce weeks 1-2. Redness calming by week 3-4.

weeks_5_8.label: Stabilisation
weeks_5_8.notes: One new product only. Wait the full 4 weeks before adding anything else.
weeks_5_8.expect: Skin more resilient. Reactivity continuing to reduce.

weeks_9_12.label: Cautious reintroduction
weeks_9_12.focus: One active at lowest possible frequency
pm_steps: Retinoid (1x per week only) OR AHA (1x per week — not both)
weeks_9_12.notes: One active, once a week. Any stinging means go back a phase.
weeks_9_12.expect: Barrier stable enough for cautious reintroduction. Still fragile — proceed slowly.

pm_routine.notes: Use lukewarm water; avoid rubbing or exfoliating cloths

pm_routine.reason: FDA-approved for rosacea; antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory

key_rules: Identify and avoid personal triggers: heat, spicy food, alcohol, sunlight, wind
Never use topical corticosteroids — risk of steroid rosacea and rebound erythema
Apply azelaic acid consistently for 3–4 months before assessing full response
Mineral sunscreen daily is mandatory to prevent UV-triggered flares
Introduce new products one at a time to identify irritants
red_flags: Worsening redness, burning or pustules despite 8 weeks of routine — seek dermatologist review
Any use of topical steroids — discontinue immediately, risk of steroid rosacea
Ocular symptoms (redness, grittiness) may indicate ocular rosacea — urgent review needed
Severe skin thickening or nodularity may indicate phymatous subtype requiring specialist care

weeks_1_4.label: Trigger identification
weeks_1_4.focus: Bare minimum while identifying personal triggers
am_steps: Mineral SPF 50 (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide)
weeks_1_4.notes: Avoid: fragrances, alcohol, menthol, witch hazel, eucalyptus. Keep a trigger diary in the app.
weeks_1_4.expect: Flares may continue while triggers are being identified.

weeks_5_8.label: Calming actives
weeks_5_8.notes: Azelaic acid has strong evidence for rosacea. Niacinamide calms vascular reactivity.
weeks_5_8.expect: Reduction in baseline redness by weeks 6-8. Flare frequency may reduce.

weeks_9_12.label: Maintenance
weeks_9_12.focus: Consistent routine. Cautious vitamin C introduction.
weeks_9_12.notes: Vitamin C tolerated by some rosacea patients at 10% — patch test on jawline first. Avoid retinoids unless prescribed.
weeks_9_12.expect: Controlled baseline. Flares manageable. Avoid retinoids — can trigger flares.
